name: Yemba
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Harro, Gretchen & Nancy Haynes. 1991. Grammar Sketch of Yemba. Yaounde: SIL Cameroon

new_statements.quote: The considerable interest in the language has focussed almost solely on tone, stemming from work by Hyman & Tadadjeu (1976). [...] In this and subsequent displays, acute and grave accent symbolise high and low tone respectively. The exclamation point symbolises downstep. [...] The English stress is usually preserved in the tone melody of the word (38a), though not always (38b). [...] Generalising across these two cases, we can observe that high tone is assigned to the penultimate vowel.
new_statements.citation: Bird, Steven. 1999. Dschang syllable structure. In H. van der Hulst & N. A. Ritter (eds.), The Syllable: Views and Facts, 447-476. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter (author preprint, May 1997, cogprints 2183).
new_statements.locator: Preprint p. 1 (sec. 1 Introduction and fn. 2) and p. 25 (sec. 6 Loanword Phonology, examples 38a-b); published version pp. 447-476
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yemba/Dschang is described as a tone language (high vs. low tone plus downstep; three-level H/M/L marking in the orthography). No opened source states a word-stress rule or discusses stress in native words. The only stress-related remarks are (a) Bird 1999: English stress in loanwords is normally mapped onto the tone melody, surfacing as high tone on the penultimate vowel of the loan; and (b) Faytak & Steffman 2023 (p. 198), reporting Hyman 1985: 48, that the first syllable of the stem is the phonologically prominent position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Bird 1999 (38b): some loans (akaleta 'carrot', akalatusi 'eucalyptus', afrepan 'frypan') do not preserve the English stress in their tone melody.
new_statements.domain_note: Loanword adaptation only (Bird); stem-initial phonological prominence (Faytak & Steffman after Hyman 1985) concerns the stem, not the phonological word; Bird's data are from the main northern (Bafou) dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources treat Yemba = Dschang = Bamileke-Dschang (ISO ybb, yemb1246). Bird 1999 states (fn. 1) that his data come from 'the main northern dialect, spoken in Bafou and elsewhere'; Assoumou 1991 covers the Foreke-Dschang variety; Nanfah 2006 delimits the Yemba dialects (Bafou, Foreke-Dschang, Bamendou, Fongo-Tongo, etc.) without separate glottocodes.

sources.locator: Preprint p. 1 (sec. 1 Introduction and fn. 2) and p. 25 (sec. 6 Loanword Phonology, examples 38a-b); published version pp. 447-476
sources.note: Describes Dschang as a tone language (acute/grave = high/low tone, downstep marked with !; 'interest in the language has focussed almost solely on tone'). No statement on native word stress. Only stress mention is in sec. 6 Loanword Phonology (preprint p. 25): English stress of loanwords 'is usually preserved in the tone melody of the word', generalised as high tone assigned to the penultimate vowel of the loan; and vowel loss in akalesang 'kerosene' 'possibly in order to mimic the stress pattern of kerosene'. Data from the main northern dialect (Bafou).

sources.citation: Wikipedia contributors. Yemba language. en.wikipedia.org (accessed 2026-09-17)
sources.note: Reports three tones (high, mid, low) and cites Harro & Haynes 1991 and Bird & Tadadjeu 1997; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Kenfack Jeuguim, Léonard, Paulin Melatagia Yonta & Sandembouo. 2024. YembaTones: A syllable-tone annotated dataset for speech recognition and prosodic analysis of the Yemba language. Data in Brief 52: 109860. DOI 10.1016/j.dib.2023.109860 (gold OA; PMC10751836)
sources.note: Data paper: syllable-level tone annotations (H/M/L) of Yemba speech for ASR; no mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Faytak, Matthew & Jeremy Steffman. 2023. Voiced aspirates with mixed voicing in Yemba, a Grassfields Bantu language of Cameroon. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 53: 189-219 [pages per running heads]. DOI 10.1017/S002510032300018X (open access)
sources.note: Instrumental (audio+EGG) study of aspiration. Sec. 1.3 (p. 192): Yemba 'has been the subject of some phonological work focusing on its complex tonal phonology (see Hyman & Tadadjeu 1976; Hyman 1985)'; all syllables bear tone. Sec. 2.1 (p. 198): targets were 'in the first syllable of the stem, which is phonologically prominent in Yemba (Hyman 1985: 48)'. No word-stress rule stated; 'stress' does not occur in the text.

sources.note: Dialectometry of Yemba varieties (Bafou, Foreke-Dschang, Bamendou, etc.) on a 100-word list with tone-marked forms; nothing on stress or accent ('accentuated' occurs once in a non-technical sense).
